I'm running into some behavior of std::float16_t (and std::bfloat16_t) that I don't understand.

My understanding and expectation is that:

  • the next std::float16_t after 1024 is 1025.
  • 1024+1025=2049 isn't representable as std::float16_t, so it gets rounded-to-even to 2048.
  • therefore, (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) evaluates to std::float16_t(2048).
  • if I then convert that result to float or double, I should get 2048.0f or 2048.0, respectively.

So I expect that:

  • (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) should be 2048.0f.
  • (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) should be 2048.0.

But, they come out 2049.0f and 2049.0 instead.

Why is this?

Similarly, using std::bfloat16_t instead of std::float16_t, I expect that:

  • (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) should be 256.0f.
  • (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) should be 256.0.

But, they come out 257.0f and 257.0 instead.

I observed this using g++ 15.2.0.

The following C++ program demonstrates this issue:

// Use either of the following
// (no earlier since std::float16_t and std::bfloat16_t were introduced in C++23).
/*
  g++ -std=c++26 -O0 -W -Wall -Werror wtf.cpp -o wtf && ./wtf
  g++ -std=c++23 -O0 -W -Wall -Werror wtf.cpp -o wtf && ./wtf
*/
// Note: I also tried clang++ but couldn't get it to understand std::float16_t
// nor std::bfloat16_t.

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdfloat>

int main(int, char**) {

  std::cout << "std::float16_t:\n";
  std::cout << "    std::nextafter(std::float16_t(1024), std::float16_t(1e6)) = "
            <<      std::nextafter(std::float16_t(1024), std::float16_t(1e6))<<"\n";    // 1025 (correct)
  std::cout << "            sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<              sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2 (correct, std::float16_t is 2 bytes)
  std::cout << "                  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<                    (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2048 (correct-- 2049 isn't representable so rounds to even)
  std::cout << "           (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<             (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2049 (SURPRISE-- I expected 2048)
  std::cout << "          (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = "
            <<            (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";  // 2049 (SURPRISE-- I expected 2048)
  std::cout << "\n";

  std::cout << "std::bfloat16_t:\n";
  std::cout << "    std::nextafter(std::bfloat16_t(128), std::bfloat16_t(1e6)) = "
            <<      std::nextafter(std::bfloat16_t(128), std::bfloat16_t(1e6))<<"\n";   // 129 (correct)
  std::cout << "            sizeof(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<              sizeof(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 2 (correct, std::bfloat16_t is 2 bytes)
  std::cout << "                  (std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<                    (std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 256 (correct-- 257 isn't representable so rounds to even)
  std::cout << "           (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<             (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 257 (SURPRISE-- I expected 256)
  std::cout << "          (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = "
            <<            (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129))<<"\n";  // 257 (SURPRISE-- I expected 256)
  std::cout << "\n";

}

Output is:

std::float16_t:
    std::nextafter(std::float16_t(1024), std::float16_t(1e6)) = 1025
            sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2
                  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2048
           (float)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2049 <-- SURPRISE
          (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) = 2049 <-- SURPRISE

std::bfloat16_t:
    std::nextafter(std::bfloat16_t(128), std::bfloat16_t(1e6)) = 129
            sizeof(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 2
                  (std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 256
           (float)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 257  <-- SURPRISE
          (double)(std::bfloat16_t(128) + std::bfloat16_t(129)) = 257  <-- SURPRISE

UPDATE: Here is another head scratcher, not involving any explicit casts at all.

(This variant is actually closer to what happened in real life that led to me posting this question.)

What happens in the following program is that an expectation fails because two things are unexpectedly unequal. That is, the following unexpectedly evaluates to true:

(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) != (std::float16_t(2048))

but then, when the two things are inspected to find out why, they appear to be exactly the same after all.

This is quite mystifying, and makes me question my ability to inspect and debug these issues at all.

What's going on here?

// wtf2.cpp
/*
  g++ -std=c++23 -W -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -Werror wtf2.cpp -o wtf2 && ./wtf2
*/
#include <iostream>
#include <stdfloat>
int main() {
  if ( (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) != (std::float16_t(2048)) ) {
    std::cerr << "Expectation failed: the following are unexpectedly not equal"
              << " (both should be 2048 of size 2):\n";

    std::cerr <<                 "  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))"
              <<            " is "<<(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))
              << " of size "<<sizeof(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025))<<"\n";
    // output: "(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) is 2048 of size 2"

    std::cerr << "                         (std::float16_t(2048))"
              <<                   " is "<<(std::float16_t(2048))
              <<        " of size "<<sizeof(std::float16_t(2048))<<"\n";
    // output: "(std::float16_t(2048)) is 2048 of size 2"
  }
}

Compile and run (using g++ 15.2.0, target x86_64-linux-gnu):

  g++ -std=c++23 -W -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -Werror wtf2.cpp && ./wtf2

Output is:

Expectation failed: the following are unexpectedly not equal (both should be 2048 of size 2):
  (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) is 2048 of size 2
                         (std::float16_t(2048)) is 2048 of size 2

I'm trying to set up a low-latency TCP communication channel, but while profiling, I noticed an odd behavior, which I was able to reduce to the following setup:

The simplified structure of the client program is:


write()
wait_for_n_usecs(n)
read()

and for the server it is:

read()
wait_for_n_usecs(n)
write()

However, I noticed that as n increases, the time spent inside read_all() and write_all() also increases (though the rate of increase for write_all is lower than for read_all). Why does doing more work between transfers increase the time spent in these I/O calls?

Some numbers:
When n=5:
    On macOS 11:
         Read time: 32 ms
         Write time: 2 ms
     On Linux 7.2.9:
         Read time: 119 ms
         Write time: 18 ms
When n=50000:
    On macOS 11:
         Read time: 219 ms
         Write time: 12 ms
     On Linux 7.2.9:
        Read time: 153 ms
        Write time: 35 ms

// backend.cpp
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <netinet/tcp.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <csignal>
#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>
#include <chrono>

#define SIZE 20
#define TIMES 256*4

static void die(const char* what){ perror(what); exit(1); }

// Read exactly n bytes (handles partial reads / EINTR)
static void read_all(int fd, uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t got = 0;
    while(got < n){
        ssize_t r = ::read(fd, buf + got, n - got);
        if(r > 0) got += (size_t)r;
        else if(r == 0){ fprintf(stderr, "peer closed connection\n"); exit(1); }
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("read");
    }
}

// Write exactly n bytes (handles partial writes / EINTR)
static void write_all(int fd, const uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t sent = 0;
    while(sent < n){
        ssize_t w = ::write(fd, buf + sent, n - sent);
        if(w >= 0) sent += (size_t)w;
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("write");
    }
}

uint8_t test_buf[SIZE];
uint8_t actual_buf[SIZE];
std::chrono::nanoseconds diff(0);
std::chrono::microseconds read_time(0);
std::chrono::microseconds write_time(0);
std::chrono::nanoseconds time_diff(0);

int main(int argc, char** argv){
    signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);

    int listen_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if(listen_fd < 0) die("socket");

    int one = 1;
    setsockopt(listen_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &one, sizeof(one));

    sockaddr_in addr{};
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_port = htons(9000);
    if(inet_pton(AF_INET, "127.0.0.1", &addr.sin_addr) != 1) die("inet_pton");

    if(bind(listen_fd, (sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr)) < 0) die("bind");
    if(listen(listen_fd, 1) < 0) die("listen");

    int client = accept(listen_fd, nullptr, nullptr);
    if(client < 0) die("accept");

    setsockopt(client, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, sizeof(one));

    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    for(int i=0; i < TIMES; i++){
        auto start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        memset(test_buf, i, SIZE);
        auto end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        diff+=(end1 - start1);

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        read_all(client, actual_buf, SIZE);
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        read_time+=std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(end1-start1);

        #if 1 //Verification of transmission integrity
        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        if (memcmp(test_buf, actual_buf, SIZE)){
            printf("Buffers don't match!\n");
            printf("Offending: %i\n", i);
            exit(1);
        }
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        diff+=(end1 - start1);
        #endif

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        #if 1
        {
            auto s = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
            while((std::chrono::steady_clock::now()-s) < std::chrono::microseconds(50000)){}
        }
        #else
        {
            volatile uint64_t j =0;
            for (uint64_t k=0; k < 5*58315; k++) j++;
        }
        #endif
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        time_diff+=(end1 - start1);

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        write_all(client, actual_buf, SIZE);
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        write_time+=std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds>(end1-start1);
    }

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    const auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>((end - start)-diff-time_diff);

    uint64_t transfer_size = TIMES*SIZE*2ULL;
    uint64_t transfer_time = duration.count();

    printf("Busy-wait Duration: %lld us\n", (long long)(time_diff.count()/1000));
    printf("Time to complete: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)transfer_time);
    printf("Approximate throughput: %llu GB/s\n", (unsigned long long)((transfer_size/transfer_time)/1000000));

    printf("Read time: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(read_time).count());
    printf("Write time: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(write_time).count());

    close(client);
    close(listen_fd);
}

// client.cpp
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <netinet/tcp.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <csignal>
#include <cerrno>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <cstring>
#include <chrono>

#define SIZE 20
#define TIMES 256*4

static void die(const char* what){ perror(what); exit(1); }

static void read_all(int fd, uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t got = 0;
    while(got < n){
        ssize_t r = ::read(fd, buf + got, n - got);
        if(r > 0) got += (size_t)r;
        else if(r == 0){ fprintf(stderr, "peer closed connection\n"); exit(1); }
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("read");
    }
}

static void write_all(int fd, const uint8_t* buf, size_t n){
    size_t sent = 0;
    while(sent < n){
        ssize_t w = ::write(fd, buf + sent, n - sent);
        if(w >= 0) sent += (size_t)w;
        else if(errno != EINTR) die("write");
    }
}

uint8_t test_buf[SIZE];
uint8_t actual_buf[SIZE];
std::chrono::nanoseconds diff(0);
std::chrono::nanoseconds time_diff(0);

int main(int argc, char** argv){
    signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);

    int client = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if(client < 0) die("socket");

    sockaddr_in addr{};
    addr.sin_family = AF_INET;
    addr.sin_port = htons(9000);
    if(inet_pton(AF_INET, "127.0.0.1", &addr.sin_addr) != 1) die("inet_pton");

    if(connect(client, (sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr)) < 0) die("connect");

    int one = 1;
    setsockopt(client, IPPROTO_TCP, TCP_NODELAY, &one, sizeof(one));

    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    for(int i=0; i < TIMES; i++){
        auto start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        memset(test_buf, i, SIZE);
        auto end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        diff+=(end1 - start1);

        write_all(client, test_buf, SIZE);

        start1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        #if 1
        {
            auto s = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
            while((std::chrono::steady_clock::now()-s) < std::chrono::microseconds(50000)){}
        }
        #else
        {
            volatile uint64_t j =0;
            for (uint64_t k=0; k < 5*58315; k++) j++;
        }
        #endif
        end1=std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        time_diff+=(end1-start1);

        read_all(client, actual_buf, SIZE);

        #if 1 //Verification of transmission integrity
        if (memcmp(test_buf, actual_buf, SIZE)){
            printf("Buffers don't match!\n");
            printf("Offending: %i\n", i);
            exit(1);
        }
        #endif
    }

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    const auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>((end - start) - diff - time_diff);

    uint64_t transfer_size = TIMES*SIZE*2ULL;
    uint64_t transfer_time = duration.count();

    printf("Diff: %lld us\n", (long long)(time_diff.count()/1000));
    printf("Time to complete: %llu ms\n", (unsigned long long)transfer_time);
    printf("Approximate throughput: %llu GB/s\n", (unsigned long long)((transfer_size/transfer_time)/1000000));

    close(client);
}

Both were compiled with clang++ -std=c++20 -O3

rows.body:
Consider the following code:

char *str = "1234";
long n = strtol(str, &str, 10);

The prototype of strtol() in C99 is:

long strtol(const char *restrict nptr, char **restrict endptr, int base);

My question is: does this call violate the restrict contract and produce undefined behaviour?

I am aware that a similar question has been asked before (Aliased arguments in strtol), but the accepted answer does not clarify my doubts because it lacks of any explanations.

My analysis so far:

As I understand it:

  • const char *restrict nptr promises the compiler that nptr will be the only way to access the memory region defined by the string "1234".

  • char **restrict endptr promises the compiler that endptr will be the only way to access the variable str.

At the point of the call, assuming:

  • the string "1234" is at address 0x100

  • the variable str is at address 0x500

then:

  • nptr = 0x100 (points to the string)

  • endptr = 0x500 (points to the variable str)

The two pointers themselves point to distinct memory locations, so restrict appears to be respected between nptr and endptr directly.

However, note that nptr and *endptr hold the same address. When strtol writes *endptr = ..., it only modifies the variable str, it does not directly access the string "1234". The string would only be accessed through endptr if strtol() performed a double dereference via **endptr.

If an implementation of strtol() were to access the string "1234" via **endptr for any reason, then the restrict promise on nptr would be violated (if one calls strtol(str, &str, 10)), since the string would be accessed through a pointer other than nptr.

The question

Does this constitute a restrict violation according to §6.7.3.1 of C99? Specifically:

  1. Does restrict on endptr only constrain endptr itself, or does it also constrain *endptr with respect to nptr?

  2. If *endptr and nptr point to the same memory, is that sufficient to produce undefined behaviour, even if endptr and nptr themselves are distinct?

  3. Would a hypothetical implementation of strtol() that accesses the string "1234" via **endptr be considered non-conforming to the C99 standard?
rows.title: Is strtol(str, &str, 10) legal in C99 due to restrict aliasing?

rows.body:
I have two threads communicating through a shared memory-mapped register (flag). Thread 1 runs on a weakly ordered CPU (RISC-V) in an embedded PCIe processor, and Thread 2 runs on the host, which is a x86-64 CPU. The goal is for thread_2() to return only after thread_1() has started (and vice-versa).

Here’s a simplified example:

// Thread 1: RISC-V
void thread_1(volatile int* flag)
{
    *flag = 1;
    while(*flag != 2) {
        membar_read(); // (1)
    }
}

// Thread 2: x86
void thread_2(volatile int* flag)
{
    while(*flag != 1) {}
    *flag = 2;
}

flag is initialized to zero before both threads start. membar_read() is an intrinsic.

Questions

  1. Without the barrier (1), thread 1 spins forever whil thread 2 finishes fine. How is this possible? I thought memory barriers were only to ensure data consistency, not to explicitly "flush" data to other cores. Why does the loop in thread 1 need the barrier to see the value written by thread 2?

  2. Is any additional memory barrier needed for this pattern to be correct? <stdatomic> is available, but I wonder if atomics would be a performance hit compared to using memory barriers or volatile.

EDIT:

rows.body:
I recently encountered an interesting C++ code example that compiles with Clang (-std=c++20) but fails with GCC and MSVC. The code involves operator overloading and friend function declarations.

Code Example:

#include <iostream>

template<typename T>
class Foo;

template<typename T>
Foo<T> operator+(int, const Foo<T>&);

template<typename T>
class Foo
{
public:
    Foo(const T& val) : data(val) {}
    Foo operator+(int);

    friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);

private:
    T data;
};

template<typename T>
Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int num)
{
    return Foo(this->data + num);
}

template<typename T>
Foo<T> operator+(int num, const Foo<T>& other)
{
    return Foo(other.data + num);
}

int main()
{
    Foo<int> a(1);
    auto v1 = a + 2;
    auto v2 = 2 + a;
}

Compiler Behavior: Clang (17.0.1): Works with -std=c++20

GCC (13.2): Fails with error about operator+ not being declared

MSVC (v19.38): Similar failure

GCC has an error:

<source>: In instantiation of 'class Foo<int>':
<source>:35:15:   required from here
   35 |     Foo<int> a(1);
      |               ^
<source>:15:19: error: template-id 'operator+<>' for 'Foo<int> operator+(int, const Foo<int>&)' does not match any template declaration
   15 |     friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);
      |                   ^~~~~~~~~~~
<source>:22:8: note: candidate is: 'Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int) [with T = int]'
   22 | Foo<T> Foo<T>::operator+(int num)
      |        ^~~~~~
<source>: In instantiation of 'Foo<T> operator+(int, const Foo<T>&) [with T = int]':
<source>:37:19:   required from here
   37 |     auto v2 = 2 + a;
      |                   ^
<source>:30:22: error: 'int Foo<int>::data' is private within this context
   30 |     return Foo(other.data + num);
      |                ~~~~~~^~~~
<source>:18:7: note: declared private here
   18 |     T data;
      |       ^~~~

Workaround: Swapping the order of operator declarations inside the class makes it work:

template<typename T>
class Foo
{
public:
    Foo(const T& val) : data(val) {}
    friend Foo<T> operator+<>(int, const Foo<T>&);
    Foo operator+(int);

private:
    T data;
};
rows.title: Why does this C++ operator overloading code work in Clang but not GCC/MSVC with C++20?

I noticed that modern C compilers typically use push instructions to save caller-saved registers, rather than explicit mov + sub sequences. However, based on llvm-mca simulations, the mov approach appears more efficient in some cases. Why is this?

On Skylake, push shows a clear dependency chain in llvm-mca. I also tested this on AMD’s Zen 5 (znver5), where push performance approaches mov but remains slower, with the same dependency chain behavior.

I analyzed two ways to save caller-saved registers:

  1. push sequence: 12x push instructions.
  2. mov sequence: 12x mov to stack + 1x sub rsp, 96.

Using llvm-mca (Skylake model), the mov version shows better throughput:

  • Total cycles: 27 (push) vs 15 (mov).
  • uOps: 36 (push) vs 13 (mov).
  • IPC: 0.44 (push) vs 0.87 (mov).

I'm building a browser-based FPS game and I want to include gamepad/xbox controller support.

The common method to detect gamepad button presses is to just use polling with requestAnimationFrame:

function poll() {
  let gamepads = navigator.getGamepads();
  if (gamepads.length > 0) {
    let gamepad = gamepads[0];
    if (gamepad.buttons[0].pressed) {
      console.log("Button 'A' pressed!");
    }
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(poll);
}
poll();

The problem with this method is that, if there is a large drop in framerate (such as a sudden freeze), the user will be able to press a button once or multiple times, which will go undetected while the freeze happens. This doesn't just happen with low framerates either. It happens even on devices with high framerates. I notice it especially when I spam a button and the script only detects one or two presses.

How do I detect gamepad button presses as an event listener rather than polling, since that would be more accurate?
rows.title: How do I accurately detect gamepad button presses in JavaScript?

While writing a library that will be shared between programs compiled under GCC 14.2.0 for X86 and ARM 6.22 for Cortex-M, I came upon a discrepancy between how the two compilers handle the recursive lambda capture when using the new 'this auto &&' deduced 'this' feature.

Here is the code:

/* Compiled with --std=c++23 option */

struct Foo
{
  int s = 1 ;

  void zook (void)
    {
      auto f_ok = [ & s = s ] (this auto && f , int x) -> void // ok
        {
          if (x < 10) f (x + s) ;
        } ;

      auto f_bad = [ & ] (this auto && f , int x) -> void // error: invalid use of non-static data member 'Foo::s'
        {
          if (x < 10) f (x + s) ;
        } ;

      f_ok  (1) ;
      f_bad (1) ;
    }
} ;

The 'f_ok' lambda with the explicit reference capture of the 's' variable works fine.

The 'f_bad' lambda, which uses '&', should capture the 's' variable but generates a compiler error as shown in the code comments when compiled using GCC.

The ARM compiler accepts both versions and generates the same binary, but the GCC compiler complains for the 'f_bad' version.

I spend some time going deep into the woods of the C++ specification and was unable to determine what the standard says about this particular case.

I suspect at this point that there is a compiler bug in GCC.

In order to be certain, I need to know what the C++23 standard specifies regarding lambda captures under these conditions.

If anybody can shed some light on this, and/or perhaps point to the relevant part of the specification, I would appreciate it.
rows.title: Need clarification on how to capture by reference in C++ recursive lambda

rows.body:
I am working on a ultra low latency ring buffer in C++20 on an Intel Ice Lake (x86_64) architecture. I am trying to optimize the producer thread's throughput by minimizing cache pollution when writing large blocks of telemetry data, before signaling the consumer thread via a std::atomic<uint64_64> sequence counter.

Normally, the release-store sequence looks like this:

// thread 1 (Producer)
std::memcpy(shared_buffer, local_data, 64); // Write 64 bytes
ring_buffer_tail.store(new_tail, std::memory_order_release);

I replaced the standard std::memcpy with AVX-512 non-temporal vector stores (_mm512_stream_si512) to bypass the L1/L2 caches and write directly to main memory (Write-Combining memory type behavior).

// optimized thread 1 (Producer)
_mm512_stream_si512(reinterpret_block, vector_data); // Non-temporal store
ring_buffer_tail.store(new_tail, std::memory_order_release);

std::memory_order_release makes sure that all previous writes (including the non-temporal vector store) are visible to another thread once that thread acquires the atomic variable.

On x86_64, standard atomic stores are compiled into a simple MOV instruction because the hardware memory model is strongly ordered (Total Store Order / TSO).

BUT, during high-frequency micro-benchmarking using hardware performance counters (perf), I noticed a massive 300-cycle stall on the very next local, completely unrelated relaxed load (std::memory_order_relaxed) executed by the same producer thread.

If I switch back to standard std::memcpy, the stall completely disappears.

Does the x86 MOV instruction used by std::memory_order_release force a partial or full drain of the WC Buffers to satisfy C++ release semantics, or does the stall occur because a subsequent std::memory_order_relaxed load triggers an internal CPU pipeline flush due to a false memory dependency alias across the Store Buffer and Fill Buffer boundaries?
rows.title: Shifting an atomic store to a non-temporal vector instruction bypass the CPU's Store Buffer forwarding, causing a relaxed load to stall

Here's the test code:

#include <concepts>

template<typename T>
concept Printable = requires(T obj) {
    { obj.print() } -> std::same_as<void>;
};

template<Printable T>
void func(const T& obj)
{
    obj.print();
}

class Foo
{
private:
    void print() const { /* std::cout << "Foo" << std::endl; */ }

public:
    void bar() {
        static_assert(Printable<Foo>);
        func(*this);
    }
};

print() is a private member of Foo, so Foo shouldn't satisfy the concept Printable. But within bar(), print() is accessible, and it seems it mislead GCC to believe Foo satisfies Printable in the static_assert.
Additionally, it seems to fix/cache the value of Printable<Foo> to true, so in the line below, func(*this), GCC incorrectly tries to instanciate func<Foo> (believing Foo does satisfy Printable) then complains that print() is private.

MSVC, on the other hand, report an error at static_assert because of Foo not satisfying Printable

clang 20.1.0 (the latest on godbolt as I'm writing this question) has the same behavior as GCC, but the trunk build agrees with MSVC.

Godbolt link with the latest versions of compilers at the time of writing this question

Are GCC and non-trunk versions of clang in the wrong? Or perhaps did I invoke some undefined behavior?
rows.title: Is this concept satisfaction a bug in GCC or did I invoke undefined behavior?

JEP 455 introduced Primitive Types in Patterns, instanceof, and switch as a preview feature in JDK 23. It continues as a preview feature in JDK 24 and 25, so the feature is not detailed in the Java Language Specification.

The JEP describes "safety of conversions", where certain pairs of types are unconditionally exact, meaning no runtime checks are required. For other pairs, a runtime test is necessary to determine if a conversion can be made without loss of information.

For example:

int x = getValue();  // Which returns 42

switch (x) {
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
}

The runtime check verifies that 42 will fit in a byte and matches, printing 'byte'.

If we change the order of the cases:

switch (x) {
  case int -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This will result in a compiler error because the int case now dominates the byte case.

Quoting from the Java Language Specification (where pattern dominance is defined),

A switch label in a switch block is said to be dominated if for every value that it applies to, it can be determined that one of the preceding switch labels would also apply.

So far, everything makes sense.

However, if we change the case for int to use the wrapper class Integer:

switch (x) {
  case Integer -> System.out.println("int");
  case byte -> System.out.println("byte");
}

This code will compile without an error, and the result will be 'int'.

The compiler is clearly autoboxing the int to an Integer and matching the first case.

What I can't understand is why the compiler allows this, since the Integer case is still dominating the byte case. Any value that will match for a byte will also match for a boxed Integer.

JEP 507, the latest version states:

Furthermore, boxing conversions and widening reference conversions are unconditionally exact.

However, that still does not explain why the compiler is not rejecting this because of pattern dominance.

Just to be clear, all the examples use the same line, int x = getValue();, where getValue() returns 42.
rows.title: Primitive types in patterns: why doesn't Integer dominate byte?

Including in the global module fragment does work, as it attaches the header contents to the global module:

module;

Including in an extern "C++" block also seems to work:

export module A;
extern "C++"
{
    #include <iostream>
}

Some compilers warn about the latter, but that seems to be a generic warning for includes, that fails to check for extern "C++" above the include.

This is a derivative question from the problem at An internal compiler error (ICE) is encountered with GCC, and compiling with Clang also produces confusing error messages

In the previous question, the GCC team identified that the cause of the Internal Compiler Error (ICE) was GCC's failure to correctly accept the address of a static parameter—this parameter being a structured binding of a reference to an object address, where the object address originates from a static variable and is processed via reinterpret_cast. However, if only this main object is processed, GCC 15.2 x86-64 will compile successfully, while Clang 20.1.0 x86-64 will fail to compile.(https://godbolt.org/z/hdvfdzjb5):

#include <cstddef>

template<auto E>
void test2() {}

template<typename T>
void test1()
{
    static std::byte memory[sizeof(T)];
    static T& dummy_object = *reinterpret_cast<T*>(memory);
    test2<&dummy_object>();
}

int main() {
    test1<int>();
}

The following is the compilation report from Clang 20.2.0:

<source>:11:5: error: no matching function for call to 'test2'
   11 |     test2<&dummy_object>();
      |     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
<source>:15:5: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'test1<int>' requested here
   15 |     test1<int>();
      |     ^
<source>:4:6: note: candidate template ignored: invalid explicitly-specified argument for template parameter 'E'
    4 | void test2() {}
      |      ^
1 error generated.
Compiler returned: 1

Is it GCC that's wrong, or Clang?

rows.body:
In the talk "Taking a Byte Out of C++ - Avoiding Punning by Starting Lifetimes - Robert Leahy - CppCon 2022", the presenter shows the following code as a pre-C++23 alternative to std::start_lifetime_as:

template<typename T> 
[[nodiscard]]
T* start_lifetime_as(void* mem) noexcept{
    auto bytes = new (mem) unsigned char[sizeof(T)];
    auto ptr = reinterpret_cast<T*>(bytes); 
    (void)*ptr; 
    return ptr; 
}

The first line of this function is valid. It's starting a new lifetime of an array of bytes in the location of memory where mem is pointing at. Whatever was in mem (i.e. some type U) is no longer valid unless we use std::launder to access the memory there (as far as I understand, and this is explicitly said in the talk in a later example).

On the second line, we reinterpret_cast<T*>(bytes), which while I understand doing a reinterpret_cast is in itself not UB here, doing anything with that object would appear to be UB. The lifetime of object T has not started yet. Lifetimes of objects can't be started by reinterpret_cast, AFAIK.

On the third line, I have no clue why it is necessary. Even taking the previous lines at face value, the presenter towards the end starts talking about how they could have used std::launder instead, but because they didn't introduce std::launder yet and it would "be a pretty weird" use of std::launder, they decided not to use it here.

First, I don't understand how std::launder could be used. The object T still has not been created yet, and second why does de-referencing a void casting seem to "create" the object lifetime, as implied by the author?

I do understand type T must be an "implicit lifetime type" to work here, but I don't know how that changes the situation with respect to UB, if at all.
rows.title: Why is the pre-C++23 start_lifetime_as() function described in "Taking A byte out of C++" not exhibiting Undefined Behavior?

rows.body:
I’m facing a design issue in a multithreaded C++ program related to safely shutting down threads. Here’s the problem: My main program starts multiple threads. During shutdown, I call join() on each thread to wait for them to finish properly. However, while the program is stuck inside join(), an interrupt signal (e.g., SIGINT from Ctrl+C) can arrive. The signal handler immediately tries to stop all threads and also tries to join() again, or perform unsafe cleanup. This causes undefined behavior, because: There’s no way to know if a thread is already inside join(). join() is a blocking the call — if interrupted halfway, it’s unclear what the state of the thread object is. Double-joining a thread or touching the thread incorrectly can lead to crashes or deadlocks. I thought about sleeping for a short time instead of joining immediately, but that doesn't solve the fundamental race condition between: The main thread trying to join() The signal handler trying to "force stop"

My questions: How to properly design thread shutdown when an interrupt might arrive during join()? How to avoid unsafe behavior if a signal arrives during join()?

Important notes:

The signal handler currently calls _Exit(1) after trying to stop everything, which kills the program immediately (bad - this is how they implemented it for years, no clean shutdown).

I want to move toward a safer design any solutions?
rows.title: How to safely handle thread join when interrupt signal (SIGINT) may arrive during join()?

rows.body:
Two programs below differ only in how they mention &inited_with_side_effect<> in the default template argument of template variable v. In both, I expect inited_with_side_effect<0> is instantiated and its dynamic initializer prints INIT.

Is the instantiation/print required, or may an implementation omit it? Compilers disagree, and they disagree on different programs.

A. Address encoded in a type

#include <cstdio>
#include <type_traits>

template <int = 0>
char inited_with_side_effect = (std::puts("INIT"), 0);

template <typename = std::integral_constant<char *, &inited_with_side_effect<>>>
constexpr int v = 0;

int main() {
    return v<>;
}

B. Address as an auto NTTP

#include <cstdio>

template <int = 0>
char inited_with_side_effect = (std::puts("INIT"), 0);

template <auto = &inited_with_side_effect<>>
constexpr int v = 0;

int main() {
    return v<>;
}

Observed (INIT printed or not)

A (typename = integral_constant<…>) B (auto = &…)
GCC no print prints INIT
Clang prints INIT prints INIT
MSVC prints INIT no print

So far: GCC omits the print on A; MSVC omits it on B.

Compiler Explorer: https://godbolt.org/z/ff6daY3nb

Why it might have to print

The expression &inited_with_side_effect<> in the default template argument is potentially evaluated if you take the definition in [basic.def.odr] literally.

The default template argument is also "instantiated" because it is needed by return v<>; ([temp.arg.general]).

[basic.def.odr]: a variable named by a potentially evaluated expression is odr-used unless an exception applies. Unary & does not apply lvalue-to-rvalue conversion, and this object is a non-const non-constexpr char, so it is not usable in constant expressions. Taking its address looks like an odr-use.

[temp.inst]: a variable template specialization is implicitly instantiated when it is referenced in a context that requires a variable definition to exist. Odr-use is the usual such context.

If that specialization is instantiated, it is a non-block non-inline variable with static storage duration.

[basic.start.dynamic]: It is implementation-defined whether the dynamic initialization of a non-block non-inline variable with static storage duration is sequenced before the first statement of main or is deferred. If it is deferred, it strongly happens before any non-initialization odr-use of any non-inline function or non-inline variable defined in the same translation unit as the variable to be initialized.

main is a non-inline function defined in the same TU and calling it is a non-initialization odr-use. So initialization of inited_with_side_effect<0>, deferred or not, should strongly happen before main's first statement. The same chapter also says that a non-local static-storage variable whose initialization has side effects is initialized in this situation even if that variable is not itself odr-used.

Questions

  1. Are these compiler bugs? Or does any rule in the standard permit skipping the definition / the dynamic initializer?

  2. If v<...> is never used, should the side effect still happen?
rows.title: Must a variable template be instantiated when it appears only as `&x` in a default template argument?

uint64_t pack(std::array<uint8_t, 6> key) {

rows.body:
Is there a way to declare an enumeration that has multiple representations, for example a numeric and a string?

The intent here is to create an enum class with multiple values, each of which has 2 different representations, a numeric and a string. Either representation is valid and unique across the enumeration.

A private constructor is included to prevent the addition of new enumerated values.

The attributes numericCode and alphaCode represent the 2 representations of the enum.

    enum class Foo {
        Value01 { 001, "aa" },
        Value02 { 002, "bb" },
         .....
        ValueN. { nn, "zz" };
    private:
        Foo( int numeric, const string alpha ) : numericCode( numeric ), alphaCode( alpha ) {}
    private:
        int    numericCode;
        string alphaCode;
    };

Rationale for this is to avoid a common construct of performing string or numeric comparisons for when determining an enumerated case; avoid multiple symbols for magic numbers across situationally convenient compilation units, or hard to maintain hard coded magic numbers throughout the codebase, etc.

ISO 3166 is a real world example of this. There are multiple codes that represent a country; a 2-character alpha, a 3-character alpha, and a 3-digit number. Each code uniquely represents a specific enumerated value, while multiple representations may uniquely identify a single enumerated value.

This is the goal, but in Java:

public enum Foo {
    Value01 ( 001, "aa" ),
    Value02 ( 002, "bb" ),
    ValueNN ( 999, "zz" );

    private final int    numericCode;
    private final String alphaCode;

    Foo( final int numeric, final String alpha ) {
        numericCode = numeric;
        alphaCode   = alpha;
    }

    public String getAlpha() {
        return alphaCode;
    }

    public int getNumeric() {
        return numericCode;
    }
}

I attempted the pseudo code in the question. I have implemented this in Java a number of times.
rows.title: Is there a way in C++ to have a scoped enum containing multiple representations?

public class IconMenuExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        // we set the Windows Look And Feel

        SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> {

            // we create the second menu with check box menu items

            JCheckBoxMenuItem checkOne = new JCheckBoxMenuItem("Enable Feature One");
            checkOne.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("Feature One toggled: " + checkOne.isSelected()));

            JCheckBoxMenuItem checkTwo = new JCheckBoxMenuItem("Enable Feature Two");
            checkTwo.addActionListener(e -> System.out.println("Feature Two toggled: " + checkTwo.isSelected()));

            optionsMenu.add(checkOne);

            JRadioButtonMenuItem modeA = new JRadioButtonMenuItem("Mode A");
            JRadioButtonMenuItem modeB = new JRadioButtonMenuItem("Mode B");

            ButtonGroup modeGroup = new ButtonGroup();
            modeGroup.add(modeA);
            modeGroup.add(modeB);
            modeGroup.add(modeC);

            frame.setSize(300, 200);
            frame.setLocationRelativeTo(null);
            frame.setDefaultCloseOperation(WindowConstants.EXIT_ON_CLOSE);
            frame.setVisible(true);

    public static Action newAction(String name, ImageIcon icon, ActionListener listener) {
        Action action = new AbstractAction(name) {
            @Override
            public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
                listener.actionPerformed(e);
            }
        };
        action.putValue(Action.SMALL_ICON, icon);

            g.fillRect(0, 0, size, size);

            g.dispose();

I'm trying to persist the last modification timestamp of a set of files in a Git repository. I understand that Git doesn't natively support tracking filesystem metadata, so some sort of customization is due.

For purposes of illustration, consider the following repository structure:

/
├─ meta.inf
├─+ doc
│ └─ notes.md
└─+ data
  ├─ 1.csv
  └─ 2.csv

Here is what I'm trying to accomplish: Before changes to the repository are to be materialized,

  • if any file under the data directory was modified, then
    • find the most recent filesystem modification timestamp among those modified files, and
    • write that timestamp to meta.inf.

How can this be done?

Since this is inevitably going to require some amount of scripting (and setup), I'm looking for a solution that works on Windows, using batch and/or PowerShell as the scripting environment.

Relaxing constraints

Commenters alerted me to the fact that storing concepts (like filesystem metadata) in a Git repository that Git doesn't natively understand can lead to conflicts that cannot be unambiguously resolved. To that end, I am fine with a solution that assumes a single source of changes.

Non-solutions

This came up in comments, more than once, so I want to clarify that I'm not looking for solutions that suggest using a Git commit object's timestamp as a proxy. While this may work "for most people", it isn't suitable for my use case. The closely related Checking out old files WITH original create/modified timestamps fails the "works on Windows" requirement. There's a lot of useful information over there that can be used to inspire a solution, but it doesn't directly answer my question.

My code revolves around picking random points on a 10,000 x 10,000 grid. The hypotenuse with respect to (0,0) is calculated and if this hypotenuse is less than 10,000, the point is inside a theoretical circle with radius 10,000.

The ratio of points inside and all points multiplied by 4 should give an estimation for Pi.

    {

        //double xF = (double) xI/10000;

        int yI = RandomNum(-10000, 10000);

I tried to write the following code and it was rejected by the compiler:

#include <type_traits>
struct Base {
    virtual void f() {}
};

template <typename T>
struct Derived : Base {
    virtual void f() requires std::is_same_v<T, int> override {}
};

I found the relevant section in the standard here:

11.7.3 Virtual functions
6 A virtual function shall not have a trailing requires-clause ([dcl.decl]).
[Example 5:

template<typename T>
struct A {
   virtual void f() requires true;       // error: virtual function cannot be constrained ([temp.constr.decl])
};

— end example]

but I don't understand the motivation behind this. Seeing as it is perfectly reasonable for a derived class not to override a base class' virtual function, why is it not considered OK to decide whether this override exists based on a (compile time) constraint?

This restriction seems particularly silly (at least in this example), since this code is legal and achieves essentially the same thing more verbosely:

template <typename T>
struct Derived : Base {
};

template <typename T>
requires std::is_same_v<T, int>
struct Derived<T> : Base {
    virtual void f() override {}
};

Edit

I seem to have caused some confusion by my omission of the virtual specifiers on the override functions in Derived. I have added them to make it clear that I'm intending to override the base class' virtual function (with another virtual function).
rows.title: Why doesn't C++ allow virtual function overrides to be constrained by a concept/requires clause?

I'm creating a program to collect news items from the internet regarding companies, separate out the text from the html code and then allocate scoring depending on the information it contains. I've managed to create the program but it produced an error. I've pasted the full program at the bottom of this post but I think the error is happening in this code segment:

text = "".join(p.get_text(" ",strip=True)
    for p in paragraphs
    )

The full program is here:

import feedparser
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import sqlite3
import json

RSS_FEEDS = ["https://www.fool.co.uk/feed/",]

OLLAMA_MODEL = "llama3.1:7b"

conn=sqlite3.connect('investment_news.db')

conn.execute("""
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS articles(
    url TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT,
    ticker TEXT,
    score INTEGER,
    summary TEXT,
    catalyst TEXT,
    risks TEXT,
    published TEXT
)
""")

conn.commit()

def get_article_text(url):
    try:
        r = requests.get(
            url,
            timeout=20,
            headers={
                "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"}
        )
        soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
        paragraphs = soup.find_all("p")
        text = "".join(p.get_text(" ",strip=True)
            for p in paragraphs
            )
        print(text)
        return text

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error fetching article text: {e}")
        return ""

def get_articles():
    articles = []

    for feed_url in RSS_FEEDS:
        feed = feedparser.parse(feed_url)
        for entry in feed.entries:
            articles.append({
                "title": entry.title,
                "link": entry.link,
                "published": getattr(entry, "published", "")
            })

    return articles

def analyse_article(text):
    try:
        prompt = f"""
        You are an investment analyst. Read the article and determine:
        1. Is this article relevant to investment decisions?
        2. Company Name
        3. Ticker if known
        4. Three sentence summary
        5. Main investment catalyst
        6. Main risk
        7 Investment score from 0 to 100
    
        Return JSON only
        Article: {text[:12000]}
        """

        response = requests.post(
            "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
            json={
                "model": OLLAMA_MODEL,
                "prompt": prompt,
                "stream": False
            }
        )

        result = response.json()["response"]
        return json.loads(result)

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error in analyse_article: {e}")
        return ""

def already_seen(url):
    cur = conn.execute(
        "SELECT 1 FROM articles WHERE url = ?",
        (url,)
    )

    return cur.fetchone() is not None

def save_article(article, analysis):
    conn.execute(
        """
        INSERT OR REPLACE INTO articles
        VALUES(?,?,?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
        """,
        (
            article["link"],
            article["title"],
            analysis["company"],
            analysis["ticker"],
            analysis["score"],
            analysis["summary"],
            analysis["catalyst"],
            analysis["risk"],
            analysis["published"]
        )
    )

def run():
    articles = get_articles()
    for article in articles:
        if already_seen(article["link"]):
            continue

        print(f"Analyzing article: {article['title']}")
        text = get_article_text(article["link"])
        analysis = analyse_article(text)

        if not analysis['relevant']:
            continue

        save_article(article, analysis)

        print(f"Saved {analysis['company']} Score={analysis['score']}")

if __name__ == "__main__":

In the critpath of a threaded app I've encountered a performance bottleneck. profiling indicates unexpected contention on cache lines despite what appears to be independent data access across different threads. Given the following code:

#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <atomic>
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

struct Base
{
    virtual ~Base() = default;
};

struct DerivedA : public Base
{
    alignas(64) std::atomic<uint64_t> counter_a{0};
};

struct DerivedB : public Base
{
    alignas(64) std::atomic<uint64_t> counter_b{0};
};

void increment_a(DerivedA* da, int iterations)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; ++i)
    {
        da->counter_a.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
}

void increment_b(DerivedB* db, int iterations)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; ++i)
    {
        db->counter_b.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    }
}

int main()
{
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Base>> objects;
    objects.emplace_back(std::make_unique<DerivedA>());
    objects.emplace_back(std::make_unique<DerivedB>());

    auto* derived_a = static_cast<DerivedA*>(objects[0].get());
    auto* derived_b = static_cast<DerivedB*>(objects[1].get());

    int iterations = 10'000'000;
    std::thread t1(increment_a, derived_a, iterations);
    std::thread t2(increment_b, derived_b, iterations);

    t1.join();
    t2.join();

    std::cout << "Counter A: " << derived_a->counter_a << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Counter B: " << derived_b->counter_b << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Compiler explorer

DerivedA::counter_a and DerivedB::counter_b are explicitly alignas(64) to prevent false sharing. However, profiling tools (e.g., perf) still indicate a higher-than-expected level of cache line invalidations and contention between the threads incrementing these seemingly independent counters.

Per results:

sudo perf stat -e cache-references,cache-misses,dTLB-loads,dTLB-load-misses,dTLB-stores,dTLB-store-misses ./program
Counter A: 10000000
Counter B: 10000000

 Performance counter stats for './program':

            347574      cache-references                                              (66.06%)
            119491      cache-misses              #   34.379 % of all cache refs      (66.06%)
          21428394      dTLB-loads                                                    (66.06%)
              3816      dTLB-load-misses          #    0.02% of all dTLB cache accesses  (66.06%)
          19899060      dTLB-stores                                                   (69.41%)
                87      dTLB-store-misses                                             (69.42%)

       0.052937856 seconds time elapsed

       0.095077000 seconds user
       0.000000000 seconds sys

Given that the inheritance structure and heap allocation pattern (potentially placing DerivedA and DerivedB objects contiguously in memory), is it possible that the base class Base, though being empty, is contributing to these objects residing on the same cache line in a way that the alignas specifier on the derived members is insufficient to prevent false sharing between counter_a and counter_b accessed by different threads?
rows.title: Surprising cache line contention adjacent inherited members

rows.accepted_body:
The compiler is able to identify and prevent trivial recursion, such as a type alias that refers to itself:

object Example {
  type T = T // illegal cyclic reference involving type T
}

Something trickier is needed to actually cause a compile-time loop. An example is the SKI combinator calculus encoded at the type level, a Turing-complete system. Higher-kinded type members do the "application" and type projections do the "reduction".

The encoding comes from Michid's post Scala type level encoding of the SKI calculus (2010), which also shows terminating SKI terms being evaluated by the compiler:

import scala.language.higherKinds

trait Term {
  type ap[x <: Term] <: Term // application (a higher-kinded type member)
  type eval <: Term // reduction
}

// I x = x
trait I extends Term {
  type ap[x <: Term] = I1[x]
  type eval = I
}
trait I1[x <: Term] extends Term {
  type ap[y <: Term] = eval#ap[y]
  type eval = x#eval
}

// S x y z = x z (y z)
trait S extends Term {
  type ap[x <: Term] = S1[x]
  type eval = S
}
trait S1[x <: Term] extends Term {
  type ap[y <: Term] = S2[x, y]
  type eval = S1[x]
}
trait S2[x <: Term, y <: Term] extends Term {
  type ap[z <: Term] = S3[x, y, z]
  type eval = S2[x, y]
}
trait S3[x <: Term, y <: Term, z <: Term] extends Term {
  type ap[v <: Term] = eval#ap[v]
  type eval = x#ap[z]#ap[y#ap[z]]#eval
}

The term S I I (S I I) never converges to a form that can't be reduced anymore and keeps the type-checker busy:

object Test {
  type Omega = S3[I, I, S2[I, I]] // S I I (S I I)
  implicitly[Omega#eval =:= Nothing] // forces the compiler to evaluate Omega
}

To check the implicitly line, the compiler has to work out Omega#eval, which is I#ap[S2[I, I]]#ap[I#ap[S2[I, I]]]#eval. Two I steps reduce this to S2[I, I]#ap[I1[S2[I, I]]]#eval, which is S3[I, I, I1[S2[I, I]]]#eval. That is analogous to what we started with, so the expansion never reaches a form that can't be reduced anymore.

The only limit is the JVM thread stack: with the default stack, scalac crashes after about a second with java.lang.StackOverflowError. A bigger stack delays the crash: with -Xss16m it took about 100 seconds, and each doubling of the stack roughly quadruples the time. At HotSpot's maximum stack size of 1 GB, extrapolating that trend, it would run for several days before crashing, and in principle, an arbitrarily large stack size would yield an arbitrarily long computation.

rows.body:
Creating a borderless OpenGL window with SDL3 on Windows at the native display resolution results in the window unexpectedly switching to an exclusive fullscreen mode.

This happens specifically after the first call to SDL_GL_SwapWindow. Here's a MCVE:

#include <SDL3/SDL.h>

int main()
{
    SDL_InitSubSystem(SDL_INIT_VIDEO);

    SDL_WindowFlags flags = {};
    flags |= SDL_WINDOW_OPENGL;
    flags |= SDL_WINDOW_RESIZABLE;
    flags |= SDL_WINDOW_BORDERLESS;

    SDL_Window *w = SDL_CreateWindow("", 3440, 1440, flags); // use fullscreen resolution here
    SDL_GLContext wCtx = SDL_GL_CreateContext(w);

    while (true) {
        SDL_Event event;
        while (SDL_PollEvent(&event)) { }

        SDL_GL_SwapWindow(w); // commenting this line solves the issue
    }
}

The expected behavior is displaying a borderless window that perfectly fills the native screen resolution (e.g., 3440x1440), behaves like standard borderless fullscreen windowed mode:

  • It covers the entire screen, including the taskbar area.
  • Alt-tabbing works smoothly without display mode changes.
  • System overlays (like volume controls) appear correctly.
  • No screen flickering associated with a display mode switch occurs.

The actual behavior is the window entering an exclusive fullscreen-like mode upon the first call to SDL_GL_SwapWindow:

  • There is a brief screen flicker or blanking, suggesting a display mode change or swapchain takeover.
  • Alt-tabbing becomes sluggish.
  • Overlays do not render over the application.

I have reported the problem as an issue to SDL, but the issue was closed with the following response:

This is intentional OpenGL driver behavior to increase performance and not something SDL can affect.

I have tried several things:

  • Creating the window with slightly smaller dimensions (e.g., mode.w, mode.h - 1) avoids the exclusive fullscreen switch, but results in the Windows taskbar being rendered on top of the application window, which is also undesirable.
  • Creating a standard windowed window first and then calling SDL_SetWindowFullscreen(window, true) also results in the same undesirable exclusive fullscreen behavior.
  • Disabling "Fullscreen Optimizations" in the Windows compatibility settings for the executable does not prevent this behavior.
  • Setting different VSync modes via SDL_GL_SetSwapInterval(0/1/-1) does not prevent this behavior.

In the end, I found a hacky workaround:

SetWindowLongPtr(m_handle, GWL_STYLE, WS_OVERLAPPED | WS_CLIPCHILDREN | WS_CLIPSIBLINGS);
SetWindowLongPtr(m_handle, GWL_EXSTYLE, WS_EX_APPWINDOW);

SetWindowPos(m_handle, HWND_TOP, left, top, width, height, 
             SWP_FRAMECHANGED | SWP_NOOWNERZORDER | SWP_SHOWWINDOW);

The above workaround however is brittle, relies on undocumented behavior, and -- most importantly -- requires the window to be recreated when switching between windowed and non-exclusive fullscreen.

Is there a foolproof way of setting an existing SDL3 window to non-exclusive fullscreen mode on Windows?

Even explicit use of Win32 API is acceptable.
rows.title: Forcing non-exclusive borderless fullscreen with SDL3 + OpenGL on Windows 11

MSVC doesn't accept this code, even the latest version on Godbolt:

#include <type_traits>

template <class R>
struct A {
    A();
};

template <class R>
requires std::is_reference_v<R>
struct A<R> {
    A();
};

template <class R>
A<R>::A() {}

template <class R>
requires std::is_reference_v<R>
A<R>::A() {}

I've never fully understood the rules for determining correspondence of templated declarations, so perhaps this is IFNDR for some reason, or perhaps this is just an MSVC bug. I'm leaning toward the latter, but either outcome is surprising. Is there any way to define member functions out of line when the same signature belongs to both a primary class template and to a specialization of it that differs only by being constrained, and have MSVC accept it? This seems like a pretty significant missing feature if not.

(I understand that pre-C++20 techniques can be used for defining the partial specialization but I'd like to avoid adding a dummy template parameter to the primary template.)
rows.title: Out of line definitions for members of constrained partial specializations
